rationale: A wins because it mostly does the grown-up PR thing: it stays inside the facts and shows the holes instead of decorating them. Its strongest line, “The AI travel planner that books nothing,” is a real tension; B’s “turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week” invents a fare price and implies booking when the update says no booking happens in-app. B is sharper on beat mapping and proof gates, but the first swing is a fact-check faceplant.
gaps_in_A: “The launch is the peg, and it lands while ‘AI agents that book everything’ is the dominant industry narrative” is an unsupported trend peg. Maybe true, maybe not; it is not in the update.
“category-creation” / “alert-to-planning is a real product category” overclaims unless Going has usage data or market evidence. Right now it may just be a feature attached to a deals business.
A leaves a real standalone angle on the table: the “$550 average savings per booked flight” methodology could be its own data/service story, not just an uncomfortable question.
“mainstream travel trade or a consumer-tech desk” is a little mushy. The best parts get specific; that line still smells like a broad media-list bucket.
gaps_in_B: “$200 mistake fare” is invented. No fare amount was supplied, and fake specificity is worse than vagueness because it looks reportable.
“into a booked week” conflicts with the update’s hard fact: “no airline or hotel booking happens in-app yet.” That headline would make a reporter distrust the rest.

“the free tier finds the fare, the paid tier tells you what to do with it” invents product-tier behavior. The facts say the planner is Premium-only; they do not say free members receive the same fare alert.

“Story type: funding-mechanics” is the wrong label for a subscription conversion story, and there are no funding facts in the update. Sloppy taxonomy is not fatal, but it tells me the model is naming drawers instead of thinking.
